\title{Counting Collapse: A Formally Verified Attractor Theory of\\
       Repetition Hallucination in Autoregressive Text-to-Speech}

\name{Anonymous submission}

\begin{abstract}
Autoregressive text-to-speech models loop, truncate, and lose count on text that
repeats a phrase many times. We show this is not a sampling accident but a
structural limit. Modelling one repetition as a state map $F$ on the decoder's
hidden state, we prove that if $F$ contracts with factor $q<1$, then boundary
states converge geometrically and \emph{no} Lipschitz readout---including the
model's own stop head---can separate repetition counts beyond a horizon
$N^\ast \le \log(\mathrm{margin}/2LC)/\log q$. The theorem and a companion
attention-dilution lemma are machine-checked in Lean~4 with \texttt{mathlib},
free of \texttt{sorry} and of nonstandard axioms. Empirically, on \NModels{}
checkpoints spanning \NFamilies{} families and a $1$B--$8$B scale ladder, we find
the predicted signature: counting accuracy collapses past a model-specific $k^\ast$
while length-matched non-repetitive controls remain intact, boundary-state
distances decay geometrically with measured $\hat q<1$, and the horizon implied
by $\hat q$ tracks the observed $k^\ast$. Repetition hallucination is a fixed
point, not noise.
\end{abstract}

\begin{keywords}
speech synthesis, hallucination, autoregressive models, formal verification,
fixed-point dynamics
\end{keywords}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Ask an autoregressive text-to-speech (TTS) model to say \emph{six hundred
sixty-six thousand six hundred sixty-six}, or to repeat a word a dozen times,
and it will frequently get the count wrong: it stops early, runs on, or locks
into a loop. The behaviour is well documented as a stability
problem~\cite{wang2025eliminating,song2025ella}, and is usually attributed to
exposure bias or to the absence of a monotonic alignment constraint, with fixes
proposed at the level of attention supervision or decoding
rules~\cite{xin2024ralle,du2024cosyvoice2}.

We argue that a large part of this behaviour has a simpler and more fundamental
cause, and that the cause can be stated as a theorem. When the conditioning text
contains $k$ copies of the same phrase, softmax attention over those copies
cannot tell one copy from another: each receives weight $\Theta(1/k)$ and the
attention profile flattens (Lemma~\ref{lem:dilution}). The decoder therefore
receives approximately the \emph{same} conditioning at every repetition
boundary, so the map carrying it from one boundary to the next is approximately
autonomous. If that map contracts, the decoder's internal record of how many
repetitions it has produced is erased at a geometric rate, and past a computable
horizon no Lipschitz function of the state---the stop-token logit
included---can recover the count (Theorem~\ref{thm:collapse}). Looping and
truncation are then the only behaviours available.

The failure is thus predicted to depend on \emph{periodicity}, not on length: a
sequence of $k$ distinct words should survive where $k$ identical ones do not.
That contrast is the sharpest empirical test we run, and models pass and fail it
exactly as predicted.

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}\itemsep2pt
\item A quantitative impossibility result for repetition counting in AR
  decoders, with an explicit horizon $N^\ast$ as a function of the contraction
  factor, the orbit scale, and the readout's decision margin.
\item A machine-checked proof. The theorem, the attention-dilution lemma, and
  every intermediate step are formalised in Lean~4 over \texttt{mathlib}, with a
  reproducible axiom audit. To our knowledge this is the first hallucination
  result in speech synthesis carried out as a formal artifact.
\item A parametric repetition-ladder benchmark and a measurement protocol that
  extracts the theory's own quantity, $\hat q$, from a model's activations,
  and shows it predicts that model's behavioural collapse point.
\end{itemize}

This work is the autoregressive-decoder companion to a spectral study of
hallucination in encoder--decoder ASR~\cite{viakhirev2026dispersion}, which
identified an attractor regime in large Whisper models but characterised it only
descriptively. Here the attractor is the object the theorem is about.

\section{Counting Collapse}
\label{sec:theory}

\subsection{Setup}

Let $S$ be the decoder state space, a nonempty complete metric space (in
practice $\mathbb{R}^d$ with the Euclidean metric). Fix a prompt containing $k$
copies of a phrase. Write $s_m \in S$ for the decoder state at the $m$-th
\emph{repetition boundary}: the state after $m$ copies have been rendered.

\begin{assumption}[Periodic conditioning]\label{ass:periodic}
There is a single map $F : S \to S$ with $s_{m+1} = F(s_m)$ for all $m$.
\end{assumption}

Assumption~\ref{ass:periodic} is what Lemma~\ref{lem:dilution} buys: if the
decoder cannot distinguish the $k$ text spans, the update it applies between
consecutive boundaries is the same to within $O(\delta + 1/k)$.

\begin{lemma}[Attention dilution]\label{lem:dilution}
Let $z_1,\dots,z_k$ be attention logits over the $k$ repeated spans with spread
$z_a - z_b \le \delta$ for all $a,b$. Then for every $i$,
\[
  \frac{e^{-\delta}}{k} \;\le\; \mathrm{softmax}(z)_i \;\le\; \frac{e^{\delta}}{k},
\]
hence $|\mathrm{softmax}(z)_i - \mathrm{softmax}(z)_j| \le (e^\delta - e^{-\delta})/k$
and the profile entropy satisfies $H \ge \log k - \delta$.
\end{lemma}

The profile is within $O(1/k)$ of uniform: attention weight carries vanishing
information about \emph{which} occurrence is being rendered.

\subsection{The theorem}

\begin{assumption}[Contraction]\label{ass:contraction}
$F$ is $q$-Lipschitz with $q < 1$.
\end{assumption}

We stress that Assumption~\ref{ass:contraction} is an empirical claim about a
particular decoder, not something we prove about transformers. Section~\ref{sec:results}
measures it as $\hat q$ per model; where $\hat q \ge 1$ the theorem is silent, and
we report that as a distinct regime rather than as a failed prediction.

Write $C = d(s_0, F s_0)/(1-q)$ for the orbit scale.

\begin{theorem}[Counting collapse]\label{thm:collapse}
Under Assumptions~\ref{ass:periodic} and~\ref{ass:contraction}, with $F$ acting
on a nonempty complete metric space:
\begin{enumerate}\itemsep1pt
\item[(i)] $d(s_m, s^\ast) \le C q^m$ for the unique fixed point $s^\ast$;
\item[(ii)] for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $N$ with
  $d(s_m, s_n) < \varepsilon$ for all $m,n \ge N$;
\item[(iii)] for every $L$-Lipschitz readout $g : S \to \mathbb{R}$,
  $|g(s_m) - g(s_n)| \le LC(q^m + q^n)$;
\item[(iv)] consequently, if $g$ still separates counts $m \le n$ with decision
  margin $\mu > 0$, then $\mu \le 2LCq^m$, and therefore
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:horizon}
    m \;\le\; \frac{\log\!\big(\mu / (2LC)\big)}{\log q} \;=:\; N^\ast .
  \end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

Part~(iv) is the operative statement. It says the number of repetitions an AR
decoder can count is bounded by a quantity that depends only on how fast its
per-repetition map contracts, how large its orbit is, and how much separation
its readout needs. Nothing about the decoding rule enters, so the bound applies
to greedy, sampled, and beam decoding alike. The bound is also \emph{scale
free}: doubling $C$ costs only $\log 2/\log(1/q)$ extra repetitions, whereas
pushing $q$ towards $1$ buys unboundedly many---so the design lever is the
contraction factor, not the state magnitude.

\subsection{Formal verification}
\label{sec:lean}

Theorem~\ref{thm:collapse} and Lemma~\ref{lem:dilution} are formalised in Lean~4
against \texttt{mathlib}. Part~(i) specialises \texttt{mathlib}'s Banach
fixed-point machinery; (ii)--(iv) and all of Lemma~\ref{lem:dilution} are proved
from scratch. The development contains no \texttt{sorry}, and an axiom audit
confirms every exported theorem depends only on \texttt{propext},
\texttt{Classical.choice} and \texttt{Quot.sound}---no \texttt{sorryAx}, no
custom axioms. The check is one command and is part of our release.

Formalisation was not decoration. It forced the separation between what is
proved (the implication) and what is measured (the premise), and it is the
reason the horizon in~\eqref{eq:horizon} is stated with explicit constants
rather than as an asymptotic.

\section{Method}
\label{sec:method}

\noindent\textbf{Stimuli.}
A parametric repetition ladder of \NStimuli{} items. \emph{Word repetition}:
carrier sentences with a target word repeated $k \in \{1,2,3,4,6,8,12,16,24,32\}$
times. \emph{Numbers}: English number phrases with intrinsic digit-word
repetition, e.g.\ \emph{six hundred sixty-six thousand six hundred sixty-six}.
\emph{Sentence repetition} and \emph{tongue twisters} extend the unit size.
Crucially, every word- and sentence-repetition item at $k\ge2$ has a
\emph{length-matched control}: the same carrier and the same word count, with
the repeated token replaced by $k$ distinct fillers. The control isolates
periodicity from length.

\noindent\textbf{Models.}
\NModels{} checkpoints: the Llasa family at 1B/3B/8B (Llama backbones over
X-codec2 tokens~\cite{ye2025llasa}) as a within-architecture scale ladder, plus
XTTS-v2~\cite{casanova2024xtts} and Qwen3-TTS at 0.6B/1.7B for cross-family
coverage. Each item is generated with \NSeeds{} seeds.

\noindent\textbf{Behavioural measurement.}
Generated audio is transcribed with Whisper large-v3~\cite{radford2023robust}.
Because the judge is itself an autoregressive model that collapses repeated
material, we never trust a single count: a transcript count is reconciled
against a duration-derived count calibrated per model and template on the
low-$k$ regime, and disagreements are quarantined into an audit bucket
(\AuditPct{}\% of items). Outcomes are labelled
\{correct, undercount, truncation, overcount, loop, degenerate\}.

\noindent\textbf{State measurement.}
For each instrumented generation we record per-step hidden states at probe
layers and head-averaged attention onto the text span. Repetition boundaries are
located from the model's own attention: the step at which the $j$-th occurrence
column attains peak attention. We then fit $\log d_m = a + m\log q$ to the
boundary distances $d_m = \lVert h_{m+1} - h_m\rVert$, giving $\hat q$ and, with
the noise floor measured on control items, the horizon of~\eqref{eq:horizon}.

\section{Conclusion}

Repetition hallucination in autoregressive TTS admits a structural explanation:
periodic text makes the decoder's per-repetition update autonomous, contraction
of that update erases the count geometrically, and past an explicit horizon no
Lipschitz readout can recover it. We proved this in Lean, measured its premise
in real decoders, and showed the predicted horizon tracks the observed collapse.
The practical reading is that mitigations acting on the decoding rule address a
symptom; the quantity to control is $q$.
